problems.statement: Is it possible from the Moon's surface to observe solar eclipses, meteors, comets, aurorae, rainbows, noctilucent clouds, artificial satellites?

solution.statement: In principle, from the Moon surface, it is possible to observe all nonatmospheric astronomical events: comets, artificial satellites and solar eclipses (by the Earth). But one can not observe auroras, rainbows, noctilucent clouds and meteors, because they take place only in an atmosphere.

problems.statement: There are Cepheid variables in all galaxies and in our own Galaxy as well. Why was the "period–luminosity" relation first established for the Cepheids in the Magellanic Clouds?

solution.statement: Because all Cepheids in the Magellanic Clouds located almost at the same distance from the Earth, their brightness is proportional to their luminosity. Therefore astronomers have found period-brightness relation for Cepheids in the Magellanic Clouds, which gave them a hint to their period-luminosity relation. Any other galaxy gives the same opportunity as the Magellanic Clouds, but all of them are far from us, and we couldn't investigate Cepheids beyond the Magellanic Clouds until recently.

problems.statement: It is known that the precession is a slow ($50''$ per year) retrograde motion of the vernal equinox points. Which of the celestial circles do these points move along – the equator or the ecliptic?

An artificial Earth's satellite moves by $6.9\,\mathrm{km/sec}$ along a circular orbit in the equatorial plane and in the direction of the Earth's rotation. What is the period of the satellite's appearance in the zenith for a point located on the equator?

solution.statement:
$$\frac{mV^2}{R}=\frac{GmM_0}{R^2},\qquad V=\left(\frac{GM_0}{R}\right)^{1/2}.$$

Taking into account $GM_0=gR_0^2$:

$$P=\frac{2\pi R}{V}=\frac{2\pi GM_0}{V^3}=\frac{2\pi gR_0^2}{V^3}\approx127\,\mathrm{min}.$$

Then:

$$\frac1T=\frac1P-\frac1{P_0},\qquad P_0=24^{\mathrm h}.$$

So:

$$T=\frac{P_0P}{P_0-P}\approx139\,\mathrm{min}.$$

Is it possible the lunar Mare Crisium whose diameter is $520\,\mathrm{km}$, to be resolved by naked eye?

solution.statement:
The Moon diameter is $3476\,\mathrm{km}$, and the visible angular diameter of the lunar disk is $31'$. Therefore, the maximum visible diameter of the Mare Crisium is

$$31'\times520/3476=4.6'.$$

This is 3–5 times more than the angular resolution limit of a naked eye. Indeed, good observers can see the Mare Crisium, that was proofed by the pretelescopic draws of the Moon.

problems.statement:
Same as for the 14–16 years old students.

In the elliptical galaxy M32 (a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy) there are about 250 million stars. The galaxy's visual brightness is of $9\,\mathrm{mag}$. If we assume that all stars there have equal luminosities, what would be the visual magnitude of one of the stars in the galaxy?

solution.statement: We can represent the figure 250 million $2.5\times100\times100\times100\times100$ which is equivalent to $1^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}=21^{\mathrm m}$. Therefore one star has brightness of $9^{\mathrm m}+21^{\mathrm m}=30^{\mathrm m}$.
